chapter: Oliver's circle and old New Orleans players
title: Jimmy Strode, Dusty Bottoms and the New Orleans musicians who could not read
summary: He recalls Jimmy Strode's carnival-style dance spot and the New Orleans musicians who came up, many of whom could not read.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: S-T-O-R-O-D-E. Conant? Yeah, Trum. He was good too. Yeah, a lot of fellows used to have him. You never heard of Nene Bryant even had him. He was a drummer, a good one. He played with Tick Chambers at Miss Cole Lawnbottom. And there was a kid around there, he died young, Jim Williams. And he used to, we couldn't go in the pool room, but he had long parents on, he had long parents. He was considered a man. And he sat on the pool room table and played for us. Now later on they said he was going to be one of the greats, but he died. He left North California, he died. But Jimmy Strode had a place they called the Dusty Bottoms. See it was like a carnival and they had all these stands around it where they chuck a luck and all that kind of stuff. And there was three card mounted and things like that. And concessions I'd say there was. And then they had this tent with the floor for dancing. It was a jitner dance, ten cents, you probably got about two minutes. And then it was cut out and then another batch would come. Well in this band they had a fellow by the name of Boudreaux, played clarinet, Ed Boudreaux. And another fellow called Percy. I know that he ascertained his last name. And then Jimmy Strode, he was from New Orleans, and Richard M. Jones, we called him Miney. You heard of him, haven't you? Oh yeah, I know. I was his cousin last Sunday. Oh he was?
And he wrote a lot of tunes too, you know.
And he played piano. So then this fellow came up that was beating out at the Irish Channel, his jaw was broken. Later on I read that he started playing the bass fiddle then. Recall.

Recall, Ellix. And then we got Lee Collins, he came up. And then Snagg Jones came up, he left, he had been playing with Celestan. And then comes Tommy Ladner. Tommy Ladner came up. So you just can see how it was with New Orleans musicians. And they were close knitted and they stuck together. And the guys said, oh this guy, they called him, called him Geechies, they called him Geechies, Cam Reed. And what they were wrong, you take people like Manny Perez, and Jimmy Noon, Eddie Atkins, and George Field, all those fellas, good musicians. And some of them were very slow, I'd say they spelled. And some of them couldn't read. So the fellas that couldn't read, if there were one fella, just like you take Paul Moria's band, a lot of those fellas didn't read either. But the piano player read. So the piano player would take and play their parts out, you know, and they'd get their parts and they still built a nice band.
